claim: Pyruvate decarboxylation is catalyzed by pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) and the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex.
source: The decarboxylation of pyruvate is a central reaction in the carbon metabolism of all organisms. It is catalyzed by the pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR) and the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a foundational fact about pyruvate metabolism.

claim: PFOR reduces ferredoxin while the PDH complex utilizes NAD+.
source: Whereas PFOR reduces ferredoxin, the PDH complex utilizes NAD+.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract describing the different electron acceptors for these enzymes.

claim: Anaerobes rely on PFOR, which was replaced during evolution by the PDH complex found in aerobes.
source: Anaerobes rely on PFOR, which was replaced during evolution by the PDH complex found in aerobes.
evidence: This is stated as established evolutionary knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Cyanobacteria possess both PFOR and PDH complex enzyme systems.
source: Cyanobacteria possess both enzyme systems.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a key observation about cyanobacteria.

claim: The cyanobacterial PFOR is stable in the presence of oxygen in vitro.
source: Instead, we show, that the cyanobacterial PFOR is stable in the presence of oxygen in vitro
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by purification experiments described in the results.

claim: PFOR is required for optimal photomixotrophic growth under aerobic and highly reducing conditions.
source: Instead, we show, that the cyanobacterial PFOR is stable in the presence of oxygen in vitro and is required for optimal photomixotrophic growth under aerobic and highly reducing conditions while the PDH complex is inactivated.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by growth experiments with deletion mutants shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The PDH complex is inactivated under photomixotrophic conditions.
source: Instead, we show, that the cyanobacterial PFOR is stable in the presence of oxygen in vitro and is required for optimal photomixotrophic growth under aerobic and highly reducing conditions while the PDH complex is inactivated.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Cells rely on a general shift from utilizing NAD(H)- to ferredoxin-dependent enzymes under photomixotrophic conditions.
source: We found that cells rely on a general shift from utilizing NAD(H)- to ferredoxin-dependent enzymes under these conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by growth experiments with ferredoxin and GOGAT mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: The utilization of ferredoxins instead of NAD(H) saves a greater share of the Gibbs-free energy.
source: The utilization of ferredoxins instead of NAD(H) saves a greater share of the Gibbs-free energy, instead of wasting it as heat.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by thermodynamic calculations described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Utilizing ferredoxins instead of NAD(H) decelerates metabolic reactions as they operate closer to their thermodynamic equilibrium.
source: This obviously simultaneously decelerates metabolic reactions as they operate closer to their thermodynamic equilibrium.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an inference from the thermodynamic considerations.

claim: During evolution, ferredoxins were replaced by NAD(P)H due to their higher stability in an oxidizing atmosphere.
source: It is common thought that during evolution, ferredoxins were replaced by NAD(P)H due to their higher stability in an oxidizing atmosphere.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: The utilization of NAD(P)H could have been favored due to higher competitiveness because of an accelerated metabolism.
source: However, the utilization of NAD(P)H could also have been favored due to a higher competitiveness because of an accelerated metabolism.
evidence: This is presented as a speculative alternative explanation in the abstract.

claim: Life evolved under anaerobic conditions in an environment that was reducing and replete with iron and sulfur.
source: Life evolved under anaerobic conditions in an environment that was reducing and replete with iron and sulfur.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Hydrogen escape to space irreversibly oxidized Earth.
source: Later on, hydrogen escape to space irreversibly oxidized Earth (Zahnle et al., 2013; Catling et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Prebiotic redox reactions took place on the surfaces of FeS minerals.
source: Prebiotic redox reactions that took place on the surfaces of FeS minerals, are at present mimicked by catalytic FeS clusters in a plethora of enzymes and redox carriers (Russell and Martin, 2004; Wächtershäuser, 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ferredoxins are small, soluble proteins containing 4Fe4S, 3Fe4S, or 2Fe2S clusters that shuttle electrons between redox reactions.
source: One example are ferredoxins, that are small, soluble proteins containing 4Fe4S, 3Fe4S, or 2Fe2S clusters and shuttle electrons between redox reactions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Ferredoxins display a wide range of redox potentials between −240 to −680 mV.
source: They display a wide range of redox potentials between −240 to −680 mV and are involved in a variety of metabolic pathways (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Ferredoxins are among the earliest proteins on Earth and are present in all three kingdoms of life.
source: Ferredoxins are among the earliest proteins on Earth and are accordingly present in all three kingdoms of life (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: FeS enzymes are especially widespread in anaerobes.
source: FeS enzymes are especially widespread in anaerobes (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: 4Fe4S clusters are oxidized and degraded to 3Fe4S in the presence of oxygen resulting in inactivated enzymes.
source: The advent of oxygenic photosynthesis necessitated adaptations, as especially 4Fe4S clusters are oxidized and degraded to 3Fe4S in the presence of oxygen resulting in inactivated enzymes (Müller et al., 2012; Imlay, 2006; Jagannathan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In aerobes, FeS enzymes are commonly replaced by FeS cluster-free isoenzymes or alternative metabolic strategies.
source: In aerobes, FeS enzymes are commonly replaced by FeS cluster-free isoenzymes or alternative metabolic strategies (Imlay, 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR catalyzes the decarboxylation of pyruvate during fermentation in anaerobes.
source: One well-known example is the replacement of the FeS cluster containing pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFOR), which catalyzes the decarboxylation of pyruvate during fermentation in anaerobes, by the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex for respiration in aerobes (Müller et al., 2012; Gould et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PFOR uses ferredoxin as redox partner while the PDH complex reduces NAD+.
source: Both enzymes catalyze the same reaction, however, PFOR uses ferredoxin as redox partner and the PDH complex reduces NAD+.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PFORs are old enzymes from an evolutionary point of view.
source: PFORs are old enzymes from an evolutionary point of view.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PFORs are widespread in autotrophic and heterotrophic bacteria, in archaea, amitochondriate eukaryotic protists, hydrogenosomes as well as in cyanobacteria and algae.
source: They are widespread in autotrophic and heterotrophic bacteria, in archaea, amitochondriate eukaryotic protists, hydrogenosomes as well as in cyanobacteria and algae (Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR can be involved in the oxidation of pyruvate for heterotrophy or catalyze the reverse reaction by fixing CO2 and forming pyruvate from acetyl CoA for an autotrophic lifestyle.
source: Depending on organism, metabolism and conditions, PFOR can be involved in the oxidation of pyruvate for heterotrophy or alternatively catalyze the reverse reaction by fixing CO2 and forming pyruvate from acetyl CoA for an autotrophic lifestyle (Witt et al., 2019; Mall et al., 2018; Evans et al., 1966).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PFOR might have played a central role for the evolution of both autotrophic and heterotrophic processes from the very beginning.
source: The enzyme might have played a central role for the evolution of both autotrophic and heterotrophic processes from the very beginning (Gutekunst, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR participates as CO2 fixing enzyme in four out of seven currently known and most ancient autotrophic pathways.
source: PFOR indeed participates as CO2 fixing enzyme in four out of seven currently known and most ancient autotrophic pathways (reverse tricarboxylic acid [rTCA] cycle, reversed oxidative tricarboxylic acid [roTCA] cycle, reductive acetyl-CoA pathway, and dicarboxylate/hydroxybutyrate [DC/HB] cycle) (Mall et al., 2018; Fuchs, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PFORs contain one to three 4Fe4S clusters.
source: PFORs contain one to three 4Fe4S clusters and in general get inactivated readily by oxygen upon purification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PFORs in general get inactivated readily by oxygen upon purification.
source: PFORs contain one to three 4Fe4S clusters and in general get inactivated readily by oxygen upon purification.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: There are three reported exceptions to the rule that PFORs get inactivated by oxygen: the PFORs of Halobacterium halobium, Desulvovibrio africanus, and Sulfolobus acidocaldarius.
source: So far, there are only three reported exceptions to this rule: the PFORs of Halobacterium halobium, Desulvovibrio africanus, and Sulfolobus acidocaldarius (Witt et al., 2019; Pieulle et al., 1995; Pieulle et al., 1997; Vita et al., 2008; Kerscher and Oesterhelt, 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The PFORs of D. africanus and S. acidocaldarius are stable upon purification in the presence of oxygen but require anaerobic conditions for in vitro maintenance of enzyme activities.
source: Even though all three enzymes are stable upon purification in the presence of oxygen, anaerobic conditions are required for in vitro maintenance of enzyme activities with the PFORs of D. africanus and S. acidocaldarius.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations in the previous sentence.

claim: The enzyme of H. halobium is the only PFOR reported so far which is active under aerobic conditions in vitro.
source: The enzyme of H. halobium is the only PFOR reported so far, which is active under aerobic conditions in vitro (Kerscher and Oesterhelt, 1981; Kerscher and Oesterhelt, 1977).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In vivo studies on oxygen-stable PFORs under aerobic conditions are missing.
source: In vivo studies on these PFORs under aerobic conditions are missing.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PFOR plays an important role in aerobic cultures of an E. coli mutant in which glucose-6P dehydrogenase (ZWF) was downregulated.
source: Recently it was shown in Escherichia coli, that PFOR plays an important role in aerobic cultures of a mutant in which glucose-6P dehydrogenase (ZWF) was downregulated (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR is probably involved in redox control during stationary phase in the E. coli ZWF mutant.
source: PFOR is probably involved in redox control during stationary phase in this mutant (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR activity in E. coli crude extracts is only detectable under anaerobic conditions in vitro.
source: This finding is highly surprising, as PFOR activity in E. coli crude extracts is only detectable under anaerobic conditions in vitro (Nakayama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: There are several reports on the aerobic expression of enzymes that are assigned to anaerobic metabolism in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: There are several reports on the aerobic expression of enzymes that are assigned to anaerobic metabolism in prokaryotes and eukaryotes and therefore challenge the simplistic distinction between aerobic versus anaerobic enzymes (Gould et al., 2019; Schmitz et al., 2001; Gutekunst et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In the evolution from anoxygenic to oxygenic photosynthesis, the soluble 4Fe4S ferredoxin was replaced by an oxygen-tolerant 2Fe2S ferredoxin.
source: In the evolution from anoxygenic to oxygenic photosynthesis, the soluble 4Fe4S ferredoxin, which transfers electrons from FeS-type photosystems PSI (photosystem I) to other enzymes in anoxygenic photosynthesis was replaced by an oxygen-tolerant 2Fe2S ferredoxin (Jagannathan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: NAD(P)H has gained importance as alternative, oxygen-insensitive reducing agent in aerobes and thereby complemented or replaced oxygen-sensitive ferredoxins.
source: In addition, NAD(P)H has gained importance as alternative, oxygen-insensitive reducing agent in aerobes and thereby complemented or replaced oxygensensitive ferredoxins, that are useful for anaerobes (Gould et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The PDH complex is composed of three subunits: PDH (E1), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).
source: The PDH complex, which utilizes NAD+ is composed of the three subunits: PDH (E1), dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2), and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The PDH complex catalyzes the irreversible decarboxylation of pyruvate.
source: It catalyzes the irreversible decarboxylation of pyruvate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The PDH complex is active under oxic conditions but gets inactivated under anaerobic conditions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: The PDH complex is active under oxic conditions but gets inactivated under anaerobic conditions in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes, albeit via distinct mechanisms.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In the absence of oxygen NADH/NAD+ ratios rise as respiration no longer oxidizes the NADH coming from the PDH complex and the subsequent reactions of the TCA cycle.
source: In the absence of oxygen NADH/NAD+ ratios rise as respiration no longer oxidizes the NADH coming from the PDH complex and the subsequent reactions of the TCA cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In prokaryotes, NADH interacts with the dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3) subunit and thereby inhibits the PDH complex.
source: In prokaryotes, as for example E. coli, NADH interacts with the dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3) subunit and thereby inhibits the PDH complex (Kim et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In eukaryotes, the PDH complex gets inactivated at high NADH/NAD+ ratios via phosphorylation of highly conserved serine residues in the PDH (E1) subunit.
source: In eukaryotes, the PDH complex gets inactivated at high NADH/NAD+ ratios via phosphorylation of highly conserved serine residues in the PDH (E1) subunit (Kolobova et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 is a cyanobacterium that performs oxygenic photosynthesis and lives photoautotrophically by fixing CO2 via the Calvin–Benson–Bassham (CBB) cycle.
source: Synechocystis sp. PCC 6803 is a cyanobacterium that performs oxygenic photosynthesis and lives photoautotrophically by fixing CO2 via the Calvin–Benson–Bassham (CBB) cycle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In the presence of external carbohydrates Synechocystis metabolizes these additionally, resulting in a photomixotrophic lifestyle.
source: In the presence of external carbohydrates these are metabolized additionally, resulting in a photomixotrophic lifestyle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In darkness Synechocystis switches to a heterotrophic or under anaerobic conditions to a fermentative lifestyle.
source: In darkness Synechocystis switches to a heterotrophic or under anaerobic conditions to a fermentative lifestyle.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Pyruvate can be either decarboxylated via PFOR or alternatively via the PDH complex in Synechocystis.
source: As in many cyanobacteria, pyruvate can be either decarboxylated via PFOR or alternatively via the PDH complex in Synechocystis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PFOR is assumed to be involved in fermentation under anoxic conditions and the PDH complex in aerobic respiration in Synechocystis.
source: PFOR is assumed to be involved in fermentation under anoxic conditions and the PDH complex in aerobic respiration.
evidence: This is stated as a common assumption in the introduction.

claim: pfor is transcribed under photoautotrophic conditions in the presence of oxygen in the cyanobacteria Synechococcus sp. PCC 7942 and Synechocystis.
source: The observation that pfor is transcribed under photoautotrophic conditions in the presence of oxygen in the cyanobacteria Synechococcus sp. PCC 7942 and Synechocystis was therefore surprising but is well in line with the observation that other enzymes assigned to anaerobic metabolism in eukaryotes are expressed in the presence of oxygen as well (Gould et al., 2019; Schmitz et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by citations.

claim: Synechocystis possesses a network of up to 11 ferredoxins containing 2Fe2S, 3Fe4S, and 4Fe4S clusters.
source: Synechoystis possesses a network of up to 11 ferredoxins containing 2Fe2S, 3Fe4S, and 4Fe4S clusters (Cassier-Chauvat and Chauvat, 2014; Artz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The 2Fe2S ferredoxin 1 (Ssl0020) is essential and by far the most abundant ferredoxin in Synechocystis and is the principal acceptor of photosynthetic electrons at PSI.
source: The 2Fe2S ferredoxin 1 (Ssl0020) is essential and by far the most abundant ferredoxin in Synechocystis and is the principal acceptor of photosynthetic electrons at PSI (Bottin and Lagoutte, 1992).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: All fully sequenced diazotrophic and nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria with photosystem II contain genes coding for a PDH complex.
source: In line with this, we found that all fully sequenced diazotrophic and nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria with photosystem II (PSII contain genes coding for a PDH complex and that 56% of these cyanobacteria possess a PFOR as well).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis presented in the results section.

claim: 56% of all fully sequenced diazotrophic and nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria with photosystem II possess a PFOR.
source: In line with this, we found that all fully sequenced diazotrophic and nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria with photosystem II (PSII contain genes coding for a PDH complex and that 56% of these cyanobacteria possess a PFOR as well).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis presented in the results section.

claim: 42% of nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria possess a PFOR in addition to the PDH complex.
source: Within the group of nondiazotrophic cyanobacteria 42% possess a PFOR in addition to the PDH complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from bioinformatic analysis presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The property of holding both a PDH complex and a PFOR in cyanobacteria that live predominantly under oxic conditions is truly widespread.
source: This clearly shows that the property of holding both a PDH complex and a PFOR in cyanobacteria that live predominantly under oxic conditions is truly widespread.
evidence: This is an inference from the bioinformatic analysis presented in the results section.

claim: The PDH complex is preferred over the utilization of PFOR in cyanobacteria.
source: The analysis furthermore confirms our observation, that the PDH complex is preferred over the utilization of PFOR in cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is an inference from the bioinformatic analysis presented in the results section.

claim: The Synechocystis Δpfor deletion mutant was impaired in its photomixotrophic growth under oxic conditions in continuous light.
source: We unexpectedly found that the Synechocystis Δpfor deletion mutant was impaired in its photomixotrophic growth under oxic conditions in continuous light.
evidence: This is a primary finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Growth impairment of Δpfor was typically visible starting around days 3–6 of the growth experiment.
source: Growth impairment was typically visible starting around days 3–6 of the growth experiment (Figure 1A and 3A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figures 1A and 3A.

claim: Maintenance in the stationary growth phase was affected in Δpfor.
source: In addition, maintenance in the stationary growth phase was affected in Δpfor.
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: Under photoautotrophic conditions Δpfor grew similar to the WT.
source: Under photoautotrophic conditions Δpfor grew similar to the WT (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The oxygen concentration in the photomixotrophic cultures was close to saturation around 250 µMol O2 throughout the growth experiment.
source: The oxygen concentration in the photomixotrophic cultures was close to saturation around 250 µMol O2 throughout the growth experiment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both pfor and pdhA genes are transcribed under photomixo- and photoautotrophic conditions.
source: Studies on the transcription of pfor and the alpha subunit of the PDH (E1) of pdhA revealed that both genes are transcribed under photomixo- and photoautotrophic conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: NADH/NAD+ ratios were stable under photoautotrophic conditions in WT and Δpfor.
source: Whereas NADH/NAD+ ratios were stable under photoautotrophic conditions in WT and Δpfor they raised three to fourfold in the first 5 days of photomixotrophic growth, exactly in that period in which the growth impairment of Δpfor in the presence of glucose was most apparent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NADH/NAD+ ratios raised three to fourfold in the first 5 days of photomixotrophic growth in WT and Δpfor.
source: Whereas NADH/NAD+ ratios were stable under photoautotrophic conditions in WT and Δpfor they raised three to fourfold in the first 5 days of photomixotrophic growth, exactly in that period in which the growth impairment of Δpfor in the presence of glucose was most apparent (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The NAD(P)H and ferredoxin pools are more reduced under photomixotrophic conditions in comparison to photoautotrophic conditions.
source: In addition, in vivo NAD(P)H fluorescence measurements and estimates for the reduction level of ferredoxin using a Dual-KLAS/NIR were performed, which show that in addition to the NADH/NAD+ ratio, also the NAD(P)H and ferredoxin pools are more reduced under photomixotrophic conditions in comparison to photoautotrophic conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The recombinant dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase of Synechocystis (SynLPD) loses activity at higher NADH/NAD+ ratios.
source: Therefore, the recombinant dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase of Synechocystis (SynLPD) was tested in an in vitro assay with different NADH concentrations. The enzyme indeed loses activity at higher NADH/NAD+ ratios, whereas NADPH has no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NADPH has no effect on SynLPD activity.
source: The enzyme indeed loses activity at higher NADH/NAD+ ratios, whereas NADPH has no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SynLPD activity was completely inhibited by NADH with an estimated Ki of 38.3 µM.
source: The SynLPD activity was completely inhibited by NADH with an estimated Ki of 38.3 µM (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The SynLPD enzyme activity dropped to approximately 50% at a NADH/NAD+ ratio of 0.1.
source: Hence, the enzyme activity dropped to approximately 50% at a NADH/NAD+ ratio of 0.1 (e.g., at 0.2 mM NADH in the presence of 2 mM NAD+).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: Much higher NADH/NAD+ ratios (>0.4) were measured in photomixotrophic cells of Synechocystis.
source: Please note, that much higher NADH/NAD+ ratios (>0.4) were measured in photomixotrophic cells of Synechocystis (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: High NADH/NAD+ ratios point to an efficient inhibition of PDH activity via the highly decreased function of the E3 subunit (SynLPD).
source: This points to an efficient inhibition of PDH activity via the highly decreased function of the E3 subunit (SynLPD).
evidence: This is an inference from the enzyme activity data presented in the results section.

claim: PFOR from Synechocystis was stable under aerobic conditions in vitro.
source: Enzymatic tests revealed that PFOR from Synechocystis was indeed stable under aerobic conditions in vitro, which means that the enzyme was not degraded and kept its activity but required anoxic conditions for the decarboxylation of pyruvate (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: PFOR from Synechocystis required anoxic conditions for the decarboxylation of pyruvate in vitro.
source: Enzymatic tests revealed that PFOR from Synechocystis was indeed stable under aerobic conditions in vitro, which means that the enzyme was not degraded and kept its activity but required anoxic conditions for the decarboxylation of pyruvate (Figure 2B) as reported for the oxygen stable PFORs of D. africanus and S. acidocaldarius (Witt et al., 2019; Pieulle et al., 1995).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: fx3 (slr1828), fx4 (slr0150), fx6 (ssl2559), fx7 (sll0662), and fx9 (slr2059) could be completely deleted from the genome.
source: To this end, fx3 (slr1828), fx4 (slr0150), fx6 (ssl2559), fx7 (sll0662), and fx9 (slr2059) could be completely deleted from the genome, whereas the deleted alleles of fx2 (sll1382) and fx5 (slr0148) failed to segregate, keeping some wild-type copies.
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: The deleted alleles of fx2 (sll1382) and fx5 (slr0148) failed to segregate, keeping some wild-type copies.
source: To this end, fx3 (slr1828), fx4 (slr0150), fx6 (ssl2559), fx7 (sll0662), and fx9 (slr2059) could be completely deleted from the genome, whereas the deleted alleles of fx2 (sll1382) and fx5 (slr0148) failed to segregate, keeping some wild-type copies.
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: fx8 (ssr3184) could not be deleted.
source: Furthermore, we did not succeed to delete fx8 (ssr3184).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: Photoautotrophic growth of all ferredoxin deletion mutants was similar to the WT.
source: Photoautotrophic growth of all these ferredoxin deletion mutants was similar to the WT (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under photomixotrophic conditions deletion of either fx3, fx9, or flavodoxin (isiB) resulted in a growth behavior that was similar to Δpfor.
source: However, under photomixotrophic conditions deletion of either fx3, fx9, or flavodoxin (isiB) resulted in a growth behavior that was similar to Δpfor (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: GOGAT is present in form of two isoenzymes in Synechocystis that either utilizes reduced ferredoxin (F-GOGAT; sll1499) or NADH (N-GOGAT; sll1502).
source: Beside the PFOR/PDH complex couple, GOGAT (glutamine oxoglutarate aminotransferase) as well is present in form of two isoenzymes in Synechocystis that either utilizes reduced ferredoxin (F-GOGAT; sll1499) or NADH (N-GOGAT; sll1502).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the results section.

claim: Neither Δf-gogat nor Δn-gogat were impaired in their growth under photoautotrophic conditions.
source: Respective deletion mutants were generated (Supplementary file 1a, b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and revealed that neither Δf-gogat nor Δn-gogat were impaired in their growth under photoautotrophic conditions, whereas Δf-gogat displayed a strong growth impairment under photomixotrophic conditions in contrast to Δn-gogat and the WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Δf-gogat displayed a strong growth impairment under photomixotrophic conditions in contrast to Δn-gogat and the WT.
source: Respective deletion mutants were generated (Supplementary file 1a, b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and revealed that neither Δf-gogat nor Δn-gogat were impaired in their growth under photoautotrophic conditions, whereas Δf-gogat displayed a strong growth impairment under photomixotrophic conditions in contrast to Δn-gogat and the WT (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Photosynthetic complex I (NDH1) exclusively accepts electrons from reduced ferredoxin instead of NAD(P)H.
source: It was recently shown that photosynthetic complex I (NDH1) exclusively accepts electrons from reduced ferredoxin instead of NAD(P)H (Schuller et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Addition of glucose resulted in higher donations of electrons to PSI in the WT and ΔglgP1ΔglgP2.
source: As expected and in parts shown recently (Theune et al., 2021), addition of glucose resulted in higher donations of electrons to PSI in the WT and ΔglgP1ΔglgP2, whereas neither ΔndhD1ΔndhD2 nor Δhk were able to provide electrons from glucose oxidation to PSI (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Neither ΔndhD1ΔndhD2 nor Δhk were able to provide electrons from glucose oxidation to PSI.
source: As expected and in parts shown recently (Theune et al., 2021), addition of glucose resulted in higher donations of electrons to PSI in the WT and ΔglgP1ΔglgP2, whereas neither ΔndhD1ΔndhD2 nor Δhk were able to provide electrons from glucose oxidation to PSI (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Photosynthesis using glucose oxidation and PSI relies on the ferredoxin-dependent photosynthetic complex I.
source: Photosynthesis using glucose oxidation and PSI thus relies on the ferredoxin-dependent photosynthetic complex I.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: ΔndhD1ΔndhD2 is not able to grow in the presence of glucose and DCMU under photoheterotrophic conditions.
source: In line with this, it was shown earlier that ΔndhD1ΔndhD2 is not able to grow in the presence of glucose and DCMU under photoheterotrophic conditions (Ohkawa et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Under photomixotrophic conditions, photosynthesis and glucose oxidation operate in parallel.
source: Under photomixotrophic conditions, photosynthesis and glucose oxidation operate in parallel.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: Photomixotrophic conditions cause highly reducing conditions in the cells as visible in reduced NAD(P)H and ferredoxin pools.
source: The cells are thus flooded with electrons from water oxidation at PSII and electrons from glucose oxidation (Figure 4). This causes highly reducing conditions in the cells as visible in reduced NAD(P)H and ferredoxin pools (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The PDH complex gets inhibited at high NADH levels under photomixotrophic conditions and is subsequently most likely functionally replaced by PFOR.
source: Our data indicate that the PDH complex gets inhibited at high NADH levels under these conditions and is subsequently most likely functionally replaced by PFOR (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Low abundant ferredoxins and ferredoxin-dependent F-GOGAT are required for optimal photomixotrophic performance.
source: Furthermore, the cells seem to rely on a general shift from utilizing NAD(H)- to ferredoxin-dependent enzymes under these conditions. In line with this, low abundant ferredoxins, whose functions are still only partly understood in detail, and ferredoxin-dependent F-GOGAT are required for optimal photomixotrophic performance (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Photosynthetic complex I (NDHI) is required to feed electrons from glucose oxidation into the photosynthetic electron chain and to thereby enhance electron flow at PSI.
source: Photosynthetic complex I (NDHI) which accepts electrons from reduced ferredoxin (Schuller et al., 2019), is furthermore required to feed electrons from glucose oxidation into the photosynthetic electron chain and to thereby enhance electron flow at PSI (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: PFOR of Synechocystis is stable in the presence of oxygen but in vitro could only measure the decarboxylation of pyruvate in the absence of oxygen.
source: We found that PFOR of Synechocystis is stable in the presence of oxygen, however, in vitro we could only measure the decarboxylation of pyruvate in the absence of oxygen (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The data strongly indicate that PFOR is active in vivo under aerobic and highly reducing conditions.
source: However, our data strongly indicate that this enzyme is active in vivo under aerobic and highly reducing conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: E. coli possesses three enzyme systems to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA: the PDH complex, PFOR, and pyruvate formate-lyase (PFL).
source: E. coli possesses three enzyme systems to convert pyruvate to acetyl CoA: the PDH complex, PFOR, and pyruvate formate-lyase (PFL) (Blaschkowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The PDH complex and PFL are the principle enzyme systems to convert pyruvate to acetylCoA in E. coli, whereas PFOR is expressed at very low levels.
source: The PDH complex and PFL are the principle enzyme systems to convert pyruvate to acetylCoA in E. coli, whereas PFOR is expressed at very low levels (Blaschkowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Transcription of PFOR was shown to be enhanced under oxidative stress in E. coli.
source: Transcription of PFOR was shown to be enhanced under oxidative stress (Nakayama et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: E. coli decarboxylates pyruvate via the PDH complex in the presence of oxygen.
source: E. coli decarboxylates pyruvate via the PDH complex in the presence of oxygen.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: Under anaerobic conditions NADH levels rise and inhibit the PDH complex in E. coli.
source: Under anaerobic conditions NADH levels rise and inhibit the PDH complex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: PFL gets activated and E. coli cells switch to fermentation under anaerobic conditions.
source: PFL gets activated and the cells switch to fermentation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: PFL activation requires reduced flavodoxin which is provided by PFOR in E. coli.
source: PFL activation requires reduced flavodoxin which is provided by PFOR (Blaschkowski et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The regulation at the pyruvate node in E. coli is mainly regulated via the availability of oxygen and its concomitant requirement for redox control and ATP.
source: The regulation at the pyruvate node in E. coli is thus mainly regulated via the availability of oxygen and its concomitant requirement for redox control and ATP (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: By downregulation of glucose-6P dehydrogenase (ZWF), less NADPH was produced in E. coli, which activated the expression of PFOR and ferredoxin reductase (FPR).
source: By downregulation of glucose-6P dehydrogenase (ZWF), less NADPH was produced in E. coli, which activated the expression of PFOR and ferredoxin reductase (FPR) (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR and FPR were shown to contribute to stationary-phase metabolism in aerobic cultures in the E. coli ZWF mutant probably by converting reduced ferredoxin to NADPH.
source: PFOR and FPR were shown to contribute to stationary-phase metabolism in aerobic cultures in this mutant probably by converting reduced ferredoxin to NADPH (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR is obviously involved in redox control in E. coli ZWF mutants in the presence of oxygen.
source: PFOR is thus obviously involved in redox control in these mutants in the presence of oxygen.
evidence: This is stated as an inference in the discussion section.

claim: The production of hydrogen by the oxygen-sensitive FeFe-hydrogenase in air-grown Chlamydomonas reinhardtii algae in a fully aerobic environment is enabled by microoxic niches within the thylakoid stroma.
source: One example is the production of hydrogen by the oxygen-sensitive FeFe-hydrogenase in air-grown Chlamydomonas reinhardtii algae in a fully aerobic environment, which is enabled by microoxic niches within the thylakoid stroma (Liran et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: PFOR and the oxygen-sensitive NiFe-hydrogenase are constitutively expressed under oxic conditions in cyanobacteria.
source: Another example is the constitutive expression of PFOR and the oxygen-sensitive NiFe-hydrogenase under oxic conditions in cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: The PFOR of S. acidocaldarius could be isolated as stable enzyme in the presence of O2, however, enzyme activity measurements required the consumption of oxygen in vitro.
source: The PFOR of S. acidocaldarius could be isolated as stable enzyme in the presence of O2, however, enzyme activity measurements required the consumption of oxygen in vitro (Witt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Living cells have the ability to maintain reducing conditions in the presence of oxygen by yet unknown mechanisms.
source: It might alternatively be that living cells have the ability to maintain reducing conditions in the presence of oxygen by yet unknown mechanisms that for example consume oxygen, which is a challenge in enzymatic in vitro assays.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: Glucose is alternatively oxidized via different glycolytic routes in Synechocystis.
source: Glucose is alternatively oxidized via different glycolytic routes in Synechocystis (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: Flux analyses have shown that glycolytic intermediates enter the CBB cycle, eventually reach lower glycolysis, and finally provide pyruvate.
source: Flux analyses have shown that glycolytic intermediates enter the CBB cycle, eventually reach lower glycolysis, and finally provide pyruvate (Nakajima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Depending on the precise route taken, glucose oxidation yields distinct forms of reducing equivalents.
source: Depending on the precise route taken, glucose oxidation yields distinct forms of reducing equivalents (Makowka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Glc6P dehydrogenase (Zwf) and 6 PG dehydrogenase (Gnd) yield NADPH, whereas GAP dehydrogenase (GAPDH) yields NADH.
source: Three enzymes are involved in oxidation steps: Glc6P dehydrogenase (Zwf) and 6 PG dehydrogenase (Gnd) yield NADPH, whereas GAP dehydrogenase (GAPDH) yields NADH.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the discussion section.

claim: PFOR is the only known direct source for reduced ferredoxin in glucose oxidation beside PSI.
source: PFOR is thus the only known direct source for reduced ferredoxin in glucose oxidation beside PSI (Figure 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section.

claim: The transhydrogenase (PntAB), which is located in the thylakoid membrane utilizes proton translocation to transfer electrons from NADH to NADP+.
source: The transhydrogenase (PntAB), which is located in the thylakoid membrane utilizes proton translocation to transfer electrons from NADH to NADP+ (Kämäräinen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Electrons from NADPH could be further transferred to ferredoxin via ferredoxin-NADPH-oxidoreductase (FNR).
source: Electrons from NADPH could be further transferred to ferredoxin via ferredoxin-NADPH-oxidoreductase (FNR).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: The diaphorase part of the NiFe-hydrogenase in Synechocystis was recently shown to shuttle electrons between NAD(P)H, flavodoxin and several ferredoxins in vitro.
source: Another potential turntable for the exchange of electrons is the diaphorase part of the NiFe-hydrogenase in Synechocystis, which was recently shown to shuttle electrons between NAD(P)H, flavodoxin and several ferredoxins in vitro (Artz et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The redox potentials have been determined for Fx1 (−412 mV), Fx2 (−243 mV), and Fx4 (−440 mV).
source: Currently, they have been determined for Fx1 (−412 mV), Fx2 (−243 mV), and Fx4 (−440 mV), whereas the value for Fx4 is based on measurements of a homologue in Thermosynechococcus elongatus (Bottin and Lagoutte, 1992; Schorsch et al., 2018; Motomura et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: For 2Fe2S clusters redox potentials between −240 and −440 mV are typical.
source: Fx1–Fx6 in Synechocystis possess 2Fe2S clusters for which redox potentials between −240 and −440 mV are typical (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: For 3Fe4S clusters redox potentials between −120 and −430 mV were determined.
source: For 3Fe4S clusters as present in Fx8 (containing one 3Fe4S and one 4Fe4S cluster) redox potentials between −120 and −430 mV were determined and for 4Fe4S clusters as present in Fx7 (4FeFS) and Fx9 (containing two 4Fe4S clusters) redox potentials between −300 and −680 mV were found (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: For 4Fe4S clusters redox potentials between −300 and −680 mV were found.
source: For 3Fe4S clusters as present in Fx8 (containing one 3Fe4S and one 4Fe4S cluster) redox potentials between −120 and −430 mV were determined and for 4Fe4S clusters as present in Fx7 (4FeFS) and Fx9 (containing two 4Fe4S clusters) redox potentials between −300 and −680 mV were found (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Fx9 is of importance under photomixotrophic conditions.
source: Our data show that Fx9 is of importance under photomixotrophic conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The redox potential of Fx9 in Synechocystis has been assumed to be around −420 mV based on its interaction partners.
source: The redox potential of Fx9 in Synechocystis has been assumed to be around −420 mV based on its interaction partners (Cassier-Chauvat and Chauvat, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The replacement of FeS enzymes and ferredoxins by FeS-free alternatives and NADPH in the course of evolution is in general discussed with regard to the oxygen sensitivity of FeS clusters in connection with the shift from anoxic to oxic conditions on Earth.
source: The replacement of FeS enzymes and ferredoxins by FeS-free alternatives and NADPH in the course of evolution is in general discussed with regard to the oxygen sensitivity of FeS clusters in connection with the shift from anoxic to oxic conditions on Earth (Imlay, 2006; Gould et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The shift from anoxic to oxic conditions was among others achieved by the escape of hydrogen into space, which irreversibly withdrew electrons from Earth.
source: However, the shift from anoxic to oxic conditions went along with a shift from reducing to more oxidizing conditions. This shift was among others achieved by the escape of hydrogen into space, which irreversibly withdrew electrons from Earth (Catling et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The withdrawal of electrons and the establishment of oxidizing conditions might have been an additional important factor that triggered evolutionary changes by enabling reactions with higher driving forces.
source: The withdrawal of electrons and the establishment of oxidizing conditions might have been an additional important factor (independent of oxygen and the oxygen sensitivity of FeS clusters) that triggered these evolutionary changes by enabling reactions with higher driving forces.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: PFOR and ferredoxins might have been replaced by the PDH complex and NADH due to their potential to release larger amounts of Gibbs-free energy.
source: The idea is thus that PFOR and ferredoxins might have been replaced by the PDH complex and NADH due to their potential to release larger amounts of Gibbs-free energy (ΔG < 0).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: When competing with other organisms for resources an accelerated metabolism can be highly beneficial.
source: When competing with other organisms for resources an accelerated metabolism can be highly beneficial.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the discussion section.

claim: PDH could not be deleted from the genome indicating that this enzyme complex is essential.
source: PDH could not be deleted from the genome indicating that this enzyme complex is essential, whereas pfor was knocked out in a previous study (Gutekunst et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding presented in the results section.

claim: pfor was knocked out in a previous study.
source: PDH could not be deleted from the genome indicating that this enzyme complex is essential, whereas pfor was knocked out in a previous study (Gutekunst et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The decision to either utilize the PDH complex or alternatively PFOR might have been determined by the prioritization for high chemical driving forces.
source: The decision to either utilize the PDH complex or alternatively PFOR and along this line, the replacement of PFOR by the PDH complex in the course of evolution might have been determined by the prioritization for high chemical driving forces.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: PFOR is dispensable under photoautotrophic conditions and cells obviously prefer to decarboxylate pyruvate via the PDH complex under these conditions.
source: PFOR is in contrast dispensable under photoautotrophic conditions and cells obviously prefer to decarboxylate pyruvate via the PDH complex under these conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by experimental data.

claim: By transferring electrons to NAD+ instead of ferredoxin less Gibbs-free energy is stored.
source: By transferring electrons to NAD+ instead of ferredoxin less Gibbs-free energy is stored.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section based on thermodynamic considerations.

claim: The reaction Gibbs energy is ΔrG′m −39 kJ/mol for the reaction catalyzed by the PDH complex versus ΔrG′m −23 kJ/mol for the reaction catalyzed by PFOR.
source: However, this comes along with a higher driving force that is visible when regarding the reaction Gibbs energies of ΔrG′m −39 kJ/mol for the reaction catalyzed by the PDH complex versus ΔrG′m −23 kJ/mol for the reaction catalyzed by PFOR (Figure 4C; Noor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by thermodynamic calculations.

claim: As the redox potential of the NADH/NAD+ pool turns slowly more negative, it might reach levels that are characteristic for ferredoxin couples.
source: The idea is thus that the NADH/NAD+ pool gets reduced first prioritizing high driving forces. However, as the redox potential of the NADH/NAD+ pool turns slowly more negative, it might reach levels that are characteristic for ferredoxin couples.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: A metabolic shift to transfer electrons to oxidized ferredoxin instead of NAD+ should come along with lower metabolic rates.
source: This might provoke a metabolic shift to transfer electrons to oxidized ferredoxin instead of NAD+ which should come along with lower metabolic rates (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a speculative hypothesis in the discussion section.

claim: PFOR and low abundant ferredoxins gain importance in the stationary growth phase.
source: This idea fits well with the observation, that PFOR and low abundant ferredoxins gain importance in the stationary growth phase (Figures 1A and 3A), which is characterized by a slowing down of metabolic reactions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data shown in Figures 1A and 3A.

claim: High NADH/NAD+ ratios can inactivate enzymes that rely on this couple and thereby support the action of isoenzymes that interact with the Fxred/Fxox couple instead.
source: The shift can be regulated on several levels. Among others, as shown in this study, high NADH/NAD+ ratios can inactivate enzymes that rely on this couple and thereby support the action of isoenzymes that interact with the Fxred/Fxox couple instead.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by experimental data.

claim: A shift to more reducing conditions will alter the thermodynamic driving force of many redox reactions, and may in itself necessitate a shift in pathways.
source: In addition, a shift to more reducing conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), will alter the thermodynamic driving force of many redox reactions, and may in itself necessitate a shift in pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as an inference from thermodynamic considerations.

claim: Electron turntables as the transhydrogenase, FNR, and the diaphorase can support the shift from NAD(H) to ferredoxin utilization.
source: In addition, electron turntables as the transhydrogenase, FNR, and the diaphorase can support this shift (Artz et al., 2020; Kämäräinen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by citations.

claim: By shifting their pools of reducing equivalents, cells are able to finetune their metabolism.
source: By shifting their pools of reducing equivalents, cells are thus able to finetune their metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion section.

claim: Cells either liberate or save Gibbs-free energy and thereby either accelerate or slow down metabolic reactions, as required.
source: They either liberate or save Gibbs-free energy and thereby either accelerate or slow down metabolic reactions, as required.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the discussion section.

claim: The cyanobacterium Synechocystis encounters highly reducing conditions under photomixotrophy in the presence of oxygen.
source: The cyanobacterium Synechocystis encounters highly reducing conditions under photomixotrophy in the presence of oxygen.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the conclusion section.

claim: Cells perform a general shift in the utilization of their reducing equivalent pools from NAD(H) to ferredoxin under photomixotrophic conditions.
source: These findings indicate that cells perform a general shift in the utilization of their reducing equivalent pools from NAD(H) to ferredoxin under photomixotrophic conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the conclusion section.
